content: Encephalitis is a neurological condition characterized by inflammation of the brain parenchyma, which can result from infections, an exaggerated immune response by the host, or a combination of both. Modulating the immune response to reduce brain inflammation may improve clinical outcomes in affected patients. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), a biological agent with both anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties, has been proposed as a potential adjunctive therapy for encephalitis. The objective of this review was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of IVIG as an add-on treatment for children with encephalitis. A comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and others, was conducted up to September 30, 2016. Additional searches were performed in sources such as the Science Citation Index Expanded and the Global Health Library. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared IVIG in addition to standard care versus standard care alone or placebo. Three RCTs involving a total of 138 participants were identified. All studies included only children with viral encephalitis, and one study specifically focused on children with Japanese encephalitis. Only the Japanese encephalitis trial, which included 22 children, contributed data to the primary outcomes of the review. Follow-up in this study ranged from three to six months after hospital discharge, while the other two studies did not include follow-up data. One additional trial was identified as ongoing. For the primary outcomes, the Japanese encephalitis study showed no significant difference between IVIG and placebo in terms of significant disability (risk ratio [RR] 0.75, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.22 to 2.60; P = 0.65) or serious adverse events (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.07 to 14.05; P = 1.00). Secondary outcomes in the same study also revealed no significant differences between IVIG and placebo. For example, the risk of significant disability at hospital discharge was similar (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.67), and there was no significant difference in the Glasgow Coma Score at discharge (median score of 14 for both groups; P = 0.53). The median length of hospital stay was comparable between the IVIG group (13 days) and the placebo group (12 days; P = 0.59). In contrast, pooled analysis of the other two studies demonstrated significant benefits of IVIG in reducing the mean length of hospital stay (mean difference [MD] -4.54 days, 95% CI -7.47 to -1.61; P = 0.002), time to resolution of fever (MD -0.97 days, 95% CI -1.25 to -0.69; P < 0.00001), time to stop spasms (MD -1.49 days, 95% CI -1.97 to -1.01; P < 0.00001), time to regain consciousness (MD -1.10 days, 95% CI -1.48 to -0.72; P < 0.00001), and time to resolution of neuropathic symptoms (MD -3.20 days, 95% CI -3.34 to -3.06; P < 0.00001) compared to standard care alone. None of the included studies reported on other outcomes of interest, such as the need for invasive ventilation, duration of ventilation, cognitive impairment, adaptive functioning, quality of life, seizure frequency, or new diagnoses of epilepsy. The overall quality of evidence for all outcomes was rated as very low. The authors concluded that IVIG may provide clinical benefits for children with viral encephalitis in certain measures, such as reducing the length of hospital stay and the time required to resolve fever, spasms, neuropathic symptoms, and regain consciousness. However, for children with Japanese encephalitis, IVIG appeared to have a similar effect to placebo regarding significant disability and serious adverse events. Due to the high risk of bias and the low quality of evidence in the included studies, no definitive conclusions can be drawn about the efficacy and safety of IVIG as an adjunctive treatment for childhood encephalitis. Furthermore, the findings are limited to viral encephalitis and cannot be generalized to other forms of the condition. Future well-designed RCTs are needed to evaluate the role of IVIG in managing all types of childhood encephalitis. Additionally, there is a need for internationally standardized core outcome measures for clinical trials in this field.
